description: Castilian kingdom (1065–1230) carved from the Leonese reconquest frontier that became the most aggressive force of the Reconquista; its fusion with León (1230) under Ferdinand III created the Crown of Castile that dominated Iberian politics, capturing the great cities of Córdoba and Seville and eventually financing Columbus's Atlantic expedition.

temporal.notes: Separated from León multiple times before permanent union 1230

lifecycle_phases.description: Ferdinand I separates Castile from León (1065), establishing it as an independent kingdom. His son Alfonso VI captures Toledo (1085), the great symbolic and strategic prize of the Reconquista, but suffers catastrophic defeat against the Almoravids at Sagrajas (1086). The Almoravid invasion temporarily halts the Reconquista; Alfonso is forced to rely on mercenary commanders including Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar (El Cid), who rules Valencia (1094–1099) independently.

After the kingdoms of Castile and León are separated and reunited multiple times, Alfonso VIII defeats the Almohads decisively at Las Navas de Tolosa (1212), the battle that breaks Almohad military power. Córdoba falls to Ferdinand III (1236) and Seville (1248) in rapid succession. By 1230, when Ferdinand III permanently reunites Castile and León, only Granada survives as an Islamic state.

rise_factors.description: Castilian frontier society, the meseta plateau with its cattle-ranching economy and warrior culture, produced a militarized aristocracy suited for the Reconquista's mobile raiding warfare; the military orders (Calatrava, Santiago, Alcántara) provided disciplined permanent forces for frontier defense

The collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba into the Taifa kingdoms (1031) gave Castile the opportunity to extract tribute (parias) from weak Islamic rulers and eventually conquer them; Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) broke the last unified Almohad resistance

The vast Castilian meseta supported transhumant sheep herding organized through the Mesta guild (chartered 1273); wool exports to Flemish weavers generated consistent revenue for the crown and created a powerful pastoral nobility with interest in frontier expansion

The capture of Toledo (1085), Las Navas de Tolosa (1212), and Córdoba (1236) each opened vast new territories; the cycle of conquest, resettlement, and extraction gave Castilian kings land and revenue to distribute, maintaining noble loyalty through expansion

Alfonso X's court produced the Siete Partidas (systematic legal code), the Alfonsine Tables (astronomical tables), and the Cantigas de Santa María; this cultural patronage legitimized Castilian royalty and established Castilian Spanish as a literary and administrative language

The Mesta, Castile's sheep farmers' guild, controlled transhumant flocks of up to 3 million merino sheep whose fine wool was the most valuable textile fiber in Europe, generating export revenues that funded royal administration.

decline_factors.description: Castile suffered repeated civil wars over succession: between Sancho II and Alfonso VI (1065–1072), between Alfonso VIII and rival factions, and the catastrophic 14th-century civil war between Pedro I 'the Cruel' and Henry of Trastámara (1351–1369) which ended with Pedro's murder

The Castilian nobility accumulated vast latifundia and military retinues during the Reconquista; the great noble houses (Mendoza, Álvarez de Toledo) could field armies rivaling the crown's own, as demonstrated by the repeated 15th-century civil wars

The Black Death and subsequent plague cycles (1348, 1363, 1374) killed 30–40% of the Castilian population; the labor shortage empowered surviving peasants to demand better terms while disrupting the tax base and military recruitment that funded frontier defense

The marriage of Ferdinand and Isabella (1469) and subsequent joint governance transformed Castile from an independent kingdom into the dominant partner in a new composite Spanish monarchy, ending its existence as a separately governed entity.
